The Cottonwick grunt Haemulon melanurum is a reef-associated teleost common throughout the Caribbean and adjacent waters, where it often forms large diurnal aggregations over hard-bottom habitats. Field surveys conducted in the Florida Keys have documented that sexually mature adults of this species attain a maximum recorded body length of 33 centimeters [Li = 33 centimeters], a size that positions it as a medium-sized member of the genus Haemulon relative to larger congeners such as the white margate. The corresponding ultimate body mass derived from length-weight relationships for this population is 624.6 grams [Wwi = 624.6 grams], a value consistent with the relatively deep-bodied, laterally compressed morphology typical of grunts. This asymptotic mass is reached several years after settlement, reflecting the gradual accumulation of somatic tissue that characterizes the post-metamorphic growth phase of haemulid fishes. Observations from mark-recapture studies indicate that individuals over 30 centimeters in total length are uncommon, suggesting that fishing pressure or natural senescence imposes an effective upper size limit in these coastal environments.

Sexual maturation in the Cottonwick grunt appears to be triggered at a total length of 19 centimeters [Lp = 19 centimeters], a size commonly observed in individuals during their second or third year of life in unfished populations. At this pubertal length, the estimated body mass is 119 grams [Wwp = 119 grams], calculated from the same weight-length equation that governs the adult size range. This size at puberty is notably smaller than the asymptotic size, conforming to a life-history pattern in which reproductive activity begins well before somatic growth is complete, a trait shared with several other iteroparous lutjanid and haemulid species. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from individuals between 18 and 21 centimeters confirms that oocyte development and testicular maturation are well underway at this size threshold, though full spawning competence may require an additional few centimeters of growth before a female can produce a viable clutch.

The neonates of Haemulon melanurum emerge from the chorion as yolk-sac larvae weighing approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams], a remarkably small initial mass that reflects the minute egg size typical of broadcast-spawning marine teleosts. This weight at birth is derived from an average egg diameter of 0.85 millimeters, placing the Cottonwick grunt near the middle of the range reported for haemulid embryos. The yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves during the first few days after eclosion, with the mouth remaining closed until the yolk is nearly exhausted. First exogenous feeding typically commences around three to four days post-hatching, after the completion of yolk absorption and the development of functional jaws and retinomotor responses that enable prey detection. The transition to active feeding represents a critical bottleneck in early survival, when the tiny larva must encounter suitable planktonic prey before reaching its point of no return.

Reproductive output in this species shows a clear dependence on female body size, an important parameter when estimating population fecundity. Under environmental conditions typical of Caribbean coral reefs, with a stable water temperature of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C], an adult female produces approximately 630 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 630 eggs per spawning event], a moderate clutch size for a fish of its body mass. The frequency of such events across the spawning season is roughly one spawning event per day [F_R_i = roughly one spawning event per day], resulting in a substantial cumulative annual fecundity that amounts to a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 630 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 630 eggs per day]. This high-frequency, low-clutch-volume strategy is characteristic of many gonochoristic reef fishes that release small, buoyant eggs into the water column for external fertilisation, and it allows the species to exploit brief windows of favorable oceanographic conditions for larval dispersal and survival.

Longevity records from otolith-based ageing studies indicate that the maximum lifespan of the Cottonwick grunt is approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years] when reared at the average water temperature of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C] that prevails across its core geographic range. This lifespan is broadly comparable to that of other medium-sized grunts, though substantially shorter than the decades-long lives reported for certain deep-reef serranids. The mortality schedule appears to be relatively type-II, with juvenile survival heavily influenced by predation from piscivorous reef fishes and adult survival more strongly shaped by fishing pressure in exploited areas. The life-history strategy of this species, characterized by reproductive onset at a relatively small size and a moderate asymptotic mass, suggests a bet-hedging approach that balances current reproductive effort against the probability of surviving to future spawning seasons.
